name: Wright Flyer
fullName: Wright Flyer (Wright Flyer I / Kitty Hawk Flyer)
tagline: The first heavier-than-air powered aircraft to achieve sustained, controlled flight. Orville and Wilbur Wright flew it at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina on 17 December 1903, proving three-axis control, a purpose-built lightweight engine and propellers the brothers designed themselves from first principles.
history: After several seasons of glider testing at Kitty Hawk between 1900 and 1902 to perfect their wing-warping control system, Wilbur and Orville Wright built the Flyer in Dayton, Ohio during 1903, designing their own 12-horsepower, 179 lb petrol engine (no manufacturer would build one light enough) and hand-carving twin pusher propellers after conducting their own wind-tunnel research to correct errors in existing aerodynamic tables. The brothers shipped the aircraft to their Kitty Hawk camp and, on 17 December 1903, made four flights; the first, piloted by Orville, covered 120 feet in 12 seconds, and the fourth and longest, flown by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Only five people witnessed the flights. The Flyer was damaged by a gust of wind shortly afterward and never flown again; the Wrights spent the following years developing the more capable Flyer II and Flyer III (the latter the first practical aircraft) at Huffman Prairie near Dayton. The original 1903 Flyer was restored and, after a long dispute between the Smithsonian Institution and Orville Wright over the museum's earlier recognition of a rival claimant to first flight, was donated to the Smithsonian in 1948, where it hangs today in the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

quickFacts: The first flight, on 17 December 1903, lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet - shorter than a 747's wingspan.
All four flights that day totalled 98 seconds; a gust then wrecked the Flyer on the ground and it never flew again.
The brothers built their own 12 hp engine in their bicycle shop because no manufacturer could meet their weight target.
A feud with the Smithsonian sent the world's most important aircraft to London for 20 years - it hung in the Science Museum until 1948.
Apollo 11 carried fabric and wood from the Flyer to the Moon in 1969 - and NASA's Ingenuity helicopter carried a swatch of its fabric to Mars, where it flew again in 2021.
Only five people witnessed the first flight, and the iconic photograph was taken by a lifeguard who had never used a camera before.

overview: The Wright Flyer is the aircraft flown by Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903 - the first sustained, controlled, powered flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. The first flight covered 120 feet in 12 seconds.{{ref:si-flyer}}

The Wright brothers developed the Flyer through several seasons of glider testing and their own wind-tunnel research, solving the problem of three-axis control that had defeated earlier attempts at powered flight. The original aircraft flew four times on 17 December 1903 before being damaged by a gust of wind, and is now displayed at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.{{ref:si-flyer}}{{ref:wiki-flyer}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: Wilbur and Orville Wright came to flight through the door nobody else used. Where rivals sought inherent stability - machines that would fly themselves - the brothers, bicycle men to the core, believed a flying machine should be unstable and *controlled*, like a bike, by its rider. Watching buzzards twist their wingtips gave them wing-warping; a twisted inner-tube box gave them the mechanism.{{ref:wiki-brothers}}

Three gliding seasons at Kitty Hawk (1900-1902) turned insight into engineering. When published aerodynamic data failed them, they built a six-foot wind tunnel and re-derived lift tables for two hundred wing shapes themselves; when they coupled warping with a movable rudder in the 1902 glider, they possessed - and patented - three-axis control, the actual invention inside the invention of the aeroplane.{{ref:si-flyer}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: For the powered machine, no engine on the market was light enough - so their shop mechanic Charlie Taylor built one from scratch in six weeks: 12 horsepower, aluminium crankcase, no carburettor or spark plugs to speak of. The propellers were the deeper triumph: the brothers realised a propeller is a rotating wing, derived the theory themselves, and carved twin pusher props of roughly 80% efficiency - a figure modern analysis confirms with some awe.{{ref:si-flyer}}

The Flyer itself: 40-foot biplane wings with warping built in, canard elevator out front (chosen after a friend's fatal stall for its supposed safety), twin rudders behind, chains from the bicycle trade driving the propellers, and no wheels - it launched from a 60-foot wooden rail the brothers called the 'Junction Railroad'.{{ref:wiki-flyer}}

sections.heading: 17 December 1903
paragraphs: After Wilbur won the coin toss and over-rotated into the sand on the 14th, repairs took two days. On the 17th, into a 27 mph freezing headwind, it was Orville's turn: 120 feet in 12 seconds, photographed at the instant of liftoff by lifesaver John Daniels in one of history's most perfect photographs - the first true aeroplane flight, powered, controlled and sustained.{{ref:si-flyer}}

They flew four times that morning, alternating turns, Wilbur's final effort covering 852 feet in 59 seconds. Minutes later a gust flipped the Flyer over and wrecked it; it never flew again. The brothers walked to Kitty Hawk village and telegraphed their father: success, four flights, inform press, home Christmas.{{ref:wiki-flyer}}

sections.heading: Aftermath & Vindication
paragraphs: The world mostly shrugged - or disbelieved. The brothers flew on quietly at Huffman Prairie outside Dayton, turning the marginal 1903 machine into the fully practical Flyer III of 1905, which banked, circled and stayed up for half an hour. Not until Wilbur's 1908 demonstrations at Le Mans - executing figure-eights before stunned French aviators who had barely managed straight hops - did the world concede what had happened five years earlier.{{ref:wiki-brothers}}

Then came the bitter decade: patent wars with Glenn Curtiss that consumed Wilbur (dead of typhoid at 45 in 1912), and a feud with the Smithsonian - which insisted its own Langley Aerodrome had been 'capable' of flight first - that sent the original Flyer into exile at London's Science Museum until the Institution recanted. It came home in 1948 and hangs today at the heart of the National Air and Space Museum.{{ref:si-flyer}}

sections.heading: Legacy
paragraphs: The Flyer's deepest legacy is method: identify the governing problem, instrument your ignorance, test incrementally, trust your own data. The Wrights ran what we would now call a research program - wind tunnel, flight test, iteration - and it beat every better-funded rival on Earth. Aeronautical engineering as a discipline starts with them.{{ref:si-flyer}}

And the twelve seconds keep echoing: a swatch of the Flyer's muslin flew to the Moon in Neil Armstrong's pocket in 1969, and another rode NASA's Ingenuity helicopter for the first powered flight on another planet in 2021, 118 years after Kitty Hawk. Every aircraft in this database is a footnote to that morning.{{ref:nasa-ingenuity}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Overturned by a wind gust
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: Shortly after completing its historic first four powered flights at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, the unoccupied Wright Flyer was caught by a strong gust of wind that overturned and damaged it badly enough that it never flew again.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Fatal crash of the Wright Military Flyer at Fort Myer
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: During a US Army demonstration flight piloted by Orville Wright, a propeller blade fractured in flight and severed a rudder control wire, sending the aircraft into a nosedive. Passenger Lt. Thomas Selfridge was killed — the first fatality from a powered-airplane crash — and Orville Wright was seriously injured.
